title: My first game made with the help of Claude
author: Lewis_Hashbrown
selftext:
Proud of my first proper game made with Claude released for android phones!

Been working on this for a few months, starting from a real basic prototype with horrible looking menus and art up untill where it is now.

I'd say 90% of this was made with Claude with plenty back and forth, testing, altering etc.

A small percentage of the art is from an asset pack but majority has been made through ChatGPT imagegen and then getting Claude to make tools to extract the art from the spritesheets, this took quite a few attempts and still isn't perfect since the spritesheets chatgpt generates aren't uniform! (although it can now generate with turly alpha transparent backgrounds which is a game changer!)

I'd say the biggest advice I can give from what I've learnt making this is, get Claude to make tools for everything, art generation, Ingame testing, balancing, checking menus scale to different screen sizes, etc 

All made in the £20 pro plan.

I'd love to hear any feedback. Can download it here

https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.meadowfall

replies.author: KereeKao
replies.body:
I don't have much experience. I did spend like $500 to get 10k downloads on a game I made, and a publisher actually contacted me. This was a few years ago so not sure what $500 gets you these days.

What I did learn from the publisher is this. They just took my game, made a ad out of it, and then looked at the ctr on the ad they made for my game. If it is below some number, then they tell you to either try to improve some things about the game or make a new game that will get better ctr's.

It seemed to me, at least a few years ago, that really you should just make trailer ads and test the ctr's without even making a game as the first step lol!

replies.author: Lewis_Hashbrown
replies.body: Good to know! I think I'll try out some paid ads next week and see how they go. Sounds like you had decent success from it!

comments.author: Substantial_Fish6717

replies.author: Lewis_Hashbrown
replies.body:
Bit of a long response, got claude to write it. 

Best I can give you is the two prompts, since the value is in the rules rather than my code — mine is welded to my own engine (HTML5 canvas, everything baked into one file). The slicing logic is just image processing though, so it ports anywhere. Only the last export step changes.

**PROMPT 1 — paste into ChatGPT / your image model.** Swap only the first sentence for your own creature. Everything below it stays fixed, so every enemy in your game comes out consistent.

>

If it comes back too smooth, reply "bigger pixels, half the detail" and regenerate. If it comes back on a white background instead of transparent, reply: "Return that exact same sheet as a PNG with true alpha transparency: remove every pure-white background pixel completely, keep every character pixel fully opaque and unchanged, no halo, matte or semi-transparent fringe. Same size, same grid, same art."

**PROMPT 2 — paste into Claude Code / Cursor / whatever you code with.** This is the slicer. Every rule in it is a bug I shipped first.

>

Two things worth keeping whatever you're building in:

* **Mirror the side row in code** instead of storing left and right separately. Half the frames, and facing can't come out wrong no matter what the generator did with those rows. Mine came back mirrored more than once.
* **Turn texture filtering off** on the import, or crisp pixels turn to soup.

And run the QA script every single time. A frame passes every automated check and still looks wrong at real size next to real art.

replies.author: Lewis_Hashbrown
replies.body:
Thanks for the download!!

So for the art generation side I got it to make a work flow where it writes all the prompts into one text file. I then copy that into chatgpt, over a few iterations we found a good prompt structure to generate art I liked through chatgpt. After that made a tool / workflow again with Claude where it took the generated spritesheets, found the borders for each sprite top and bottom and spliced them into examples for me to say if they work or not (chatgpt doesn't make uniform spritesheets)

The prompt structure I stated stardew valley, large pixel like. And listed each row on a seperate line eg. ROW 1 walking left ROW 2 walking right ROW 5 attacking left Etc

https://preview.redd.it/924d1bps1jnh1.png?width=822&format=png&auto=webp&s=d99f748c55ebaf173047101bdcf0cfb18e80f861

Like the example pic, this was near the beginning of making the workflow. You can see it cropped some badly. Went back to Claude and said this and it refined how it did it. Now it pretty much gets it correct first go

replies.author: Lewis_Hashbrown
replies.body:
Example prompt. This made the attached spritesheet

======================= 12. LAVA GOLEM (Volcano map) ======================= Pixel-art sprite sheet of a bulky golem built from dark volcanic rock with molten lava glowing at its joints and core; its attack is a double-fist ground slam. Cute chunky retro RPG style (Stardew/Cute-Fantasy look). Pixel style â€” this is the most important rule: draw the character in genuine LOW-RES pixel art, as if it were only about 32 pixels tall, then upscaled \~5x with crisp square pixels (nearest-neighbor). Every visible "pixel" should be a big square block. Simple shapes, minimal shading (2-3 tones per color), no fine detail, no anti-aliasing, no smooth gradients. It must match a 16x16/32x32 retro tileset, NOT smooth high-res "HD pixel art". Canvas: 1024 x 1536 pixels (portrait). Layout: a strict grid of 4 columns x 8 rows, so every cell is exactly 256 x 192 pixels. One animation frame per cell, 4 frames per row reading left to right. Row order, top to bottom: row 1: WALK cycle, facing DOWN (toward the viewer) row 2: WALK cycle, facing RIGHT row 3: WALK cycle, facing UP (back view, facing away) row 4: WALK cycle, facing LEFT row 5: ATTACK animation, facing DOWN row 6: ATTACK animation, facing RIGHT row 7: ATTACK animation, facing UP row 8: ATTACK animation, facing LEFT Rules: - Background: solid pure white (#FFFFFF) everywhere. No checkerboard, no gradient, no drop shadows, no ground shadow under the character. - The character is about 150-170 pixels tall, the SAME size in every frame, centred horizontally in its cell, feet on the same baseline in every frame of a row. - Nothing may touch or cross a cell edge; leave clear white margin around each frame. - Each WALK row must be a REAL 4-frame walking cycle with clearly different leg poses: frame 1 = LEFT foot forward, frame 2 = feet passing together (body slightly higher), frame 3 = RIGHT foot forward, frame 4 = feet passing together. In the RIGHT and LEFT facing rows the stride must read clearly from the side: legs scissoring past each other with a small body bob. NEVER draw the same standing pose 4 times. - Left-facing rows are the mirror of right-facing rows (same pose, flipped). - Thick dark outline (near-black, never white or light grey) around the whole character. - Limited palette, roughly 8-12 colors. IMPORTANT: no pure white INSIDE the character â€” use cream/off-white or pale yellow for the hottest lava at the core and joints. Pure white is reserved for the background only. - No loose particles, dust or effects below the feet. - No text, numbers, labels, grid lines, borders or watermarks anywhere.
